# The host language

The 1446 book had no host language to explain: its letters were the whole
system. gog's letters are typed in four programming languages, and this part
says what each language adds.

Everything so far has been the same in every language, because the grammar does
not change with the language you type it in. One engine reads one specification,
so the same sentence draws the same plot in every language.

Some things belong to the language you type in rather than to the grammar, and
they cannot be stated once for everybody. How does a table reach `data()`? How
does a plot display where you work? How does gog's `+` work beside the operators
the language already has? Those are real questions. One answer in the grammar
chapters would be wrong for readers of the other three languages.

Each of the four languages has a chapter here [@rcore2026;
@vanrossum2009python; @bezanson2017julia; @ecma2025javascript]. A language's gog
package is called a *binding*. The same word also names a channel with its
column, such as `x(gdp)`; in this part, *binding* means the package. The grammar
chapters mention a language only where something belongs to that language
alone, such as R's `factor()`, and this part holds the rest.

The four chapters are ordered R, Python, Julia, JavaScript, and the order has a
reason. You write the same sentence in the first three. The operators are
identical, and the main change is the column name: a bare `gdp`, then `col.gdp`,
then `:gdp`. Values such as `TRUE` and `c("a", "b")` also take each language's
own spelling. If you have read the R in this book you can read the Python and
the Julia already. JavaScript is the one that genuinely reads differently. It is
the only one of the four that cannot give `+`, `*`, `|` and `/` new meanings, so
it spells them as words. It is last for that reason, so the pattern the other
three share is read first.

The claim that one sentence draws one plot in every language is tested. Every
sentence in this book that describes a plot was translated into each language
and drawn by its binding, and the four plots match byte for byte. The four
bindings refuse the same sentences: in the engine's own words where the engine
refuses, and in each language's own spelling where the binding refuses. The test
skips only the sentences about a host language itself, and two that write a file
rather than draw a plot.
